lessons.title: Cleaning and sorting produce for better prices
lessons.body: Buyers pay more for clean, uniform produce. Start by cleaning your harvest the same day. For vegetables like tomatoes, use a soft brush or cloth to remove soil. For root crops like carrots, wash in clean water with a little salt (1 tablespoon per 10 litres) to kill germs, then rinse. Never soak produce in water for longâit causes rot. Remove leaves, stems, and any damaged parts. Sorting means separating produce by size, ripeness, and appearance. For example, grade tomatoes into three groups: large, medium, and small. Large ones fetch 20-30% more in urban markets. Use simple tools: a plastic basin, clean water, a soft brush, and sorting trays or mats. Work in the shade to avoid sun damage. After cleaning, let produce dry in a well-ventilated area. For leafy greens like kale, remove wilted leaves and tie into bundles of 5-10 stems. Sorting also removes diseased items that can spoil the whole batch. A farmer in Kenya who sorted and cleaned her mangoes increased her price from KES 20 to KES 35 per fruit. Do this consistently, and buyers will seek you out. Remember: clean produce looks professional and reduces waste. Aim to sort within 4 hours of harvest for best freshness.

lessons.title: Grading by size, colour, and quality
lessons.body: Grading is sorting produce into uniform categories based on size, colour, and quality. Buyers like uniformity because it simplifies pricing and packaging. For size, use simple tools: a measuring tape or a wooden template with holes of different diameters. For example, grade avocados by diameter: small (5-6 cm), medium (6-7 cm), large (7-8 cm). For colour, use a colour chart or your eye. Tomatoes: green (unripe), pink (half-ripe), red (ripe). Bananas: green, yellow, spotted. Quality grades: Grade A (no blemishes, uniform shape), Grade B (minor defects), Grade C (major defects, for processing). In many African markets, Grade A fetches 50% more than Grade C. For maize, grade by kernel size and moisture content (use a moisture meter if available; otherwise, bite testâif it cracks, it's dry enough). For eggs, grade by weight: small (under 45g), medium (45-55g), large (55-65g), extra-large (over 65g). Always grade in a clean, shaded area. Use a grading table or mat. Label each grade clearly. A Ghanaian farmer who graded her pineapples by size and colour doubled her export sales. Start simple: use three grades. Be consistentâbuyers trust farmers who deliver the same grade every time. Train your workers on the same standards. Grading adds value with little cost, just time and attention.

lessons.title: Packaging in sacks, crates, or baskets
lessons.body: Packaging protects produce and makes handling easier. Choose the right container for your crop. For grains like maize, beans, and rice, use clean jute or polypropylene sacks. A standard 50 kg sack is common. Ensure sacks are dry and free of holes. For vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, and leafy greens, use plastic crates (20-25 kg capacity) or wooden crates. Crates allow airflow and prevent crushing. Avoid overfillingâleave 2-3 cm at the top. For fruits like mangoes and oranges, use ventilated plastic crates or cardboard boxes with holes. For fragile produce like eggs, use egg trays or cartons. Baskets (woven from local materials) work for small quantities and local markets. Always line containers with clean paper or leaves to reduce bruising. Never use dirty containersâthey spread disease. For transport, stack crates no more than 4 high to avoid crushing. Label each container with your farm name, produce type, grade, and weight. For sacks, use a permanent marker on a tag. A Nigerian farmer who switched from sacks to crates for tomatoes reduced losses from 30% to 10%. Packaging costs money, but it pays back through higher prices and less waste. Reuse crates and sacks when possible. Clean and dry them between uses. Proper packaging shows buyers you are serious.

lessons.title: Reducing post-harvest losses during transport
lessons.body: Post-harvest losses in Africa can reach 40% for fruits and vegetables. Most losses happen during transport. To reduce them, harvest at the right timeâearly morning or late evening when it's cool. Never transport in the heat of the day. Use covered vehicles or tarpaulins to protect from sun and rain. But don't seal completelyâleave vents for airflow. Pack produce tightly to prevent shifting, but not so tight that it crushes. Use cushioning materials like dry grass or paper between layers. For long distances, use refrigerated trucks if available, but they are expensive. A cheaper option: use evaporative cooling. Wrap produce in wet sacks or place in a ventilated box with wet sand. For example, a farmer in Senegal used wet jute sacks over vegetables and reduced losses by half. Avoid mixing different produceâethylene from ripe fruits speeds ripening of others. Keep fruits and vegetables separate. Drive carefully on rough roads; speed causes bruising. Plan your route to avoid delays. If you sell at a market, arrive early to secure a shaded spot. For short trips, use a bicycle or motorcycle with a padded box. Always handle crates gentlyâdon't drop them. After transport, unpack immediately and store in a cool place. A Kenyan tomato farmer who used crates and early morning transport cut losses from 35% to 12%. Simple steps save money.

lessons.title: Labeling and branding your produce simply
lessons.body: Labeling and branding help buyers recognize and trust your produce. You don't need expensive printing. Start with a simple label: your farm name, location, produce type, grade, and weight. Use a permanent marker on a tag or sticker. For example, 'Green Valley Farm, Nakuru, Tomatoes Grade A, 10 kg'. If you sell in bulk, put a label on each sack or crate. For packaged units (like 1 kg bags of beans), create a simple sticker with your name and contact. Branding means creating a consistent identity. Choose a name and logo. A logo can be a simple drawingâa sun, a leaf, a tractor. Use the same colours on all labels. This helps customers remember you. In local markets, a recognizable brand can get you 10-20% higher prices. For example, a Ghanaian pepper farmer used a red label with a chili logo and became known for quality. He now sells out before other vendors. You can also use social media (WhatsApp, Facebook) to show your brand. Take photos of your well-packaged produce. Tell buyers your storyâhow you grow, harvest, and pack. Honest labeling builds trust. Never lie about grade or weightâit ruins your reputation. Keep labels simple and clear. Use local language if needed. A label is your handshake with the buyer.

lessons.title: Meeting buyer quality requirements
lessons.body: Buyers have specific quality standards. Before you plant, ask your buyer what they want. For supermarkets, they may require: uniform size, specific colour, no blemishes, pesticide residue limits, and proper packaging. For exporters, standards are stricter: GlobalG.A.P. certification, traceability, and cold chain. For local hotels and restaurants, they may want fresh, clean produce delivered daily. To meet these, start with good seed and proper growing practices. Harvest at the right maturity. Clean, grade, and pack carefully. Keep records: planting date, inputs used, harvest date. This helps with traceability. For pesticide use, follow pre-harvest intervalsâdon't spray close to harvest. Use only approved chemicals. If you can't meet a standard, don't promise it. It's better to sell to a buyer with lower standards than to fail a contract. For example, a Kenyan farmer lost a supermarket contract because his tomatoes had spots. He now grades strictly and checks each fruit. To find buyer requirements, visit the buyer, ask questions, and read contracts carefully. Ask for a sample of what they expect. Attend training from extension officers or NGOs. Many buyers provide feedbackâuse it to improve. Consistent quality leads to repeat orders and better prices. Start with one buyer, meet their needs, then expand. Quality is a habit, not a one-time effort.

quiz.q: Why is cleaning produce important for market?
options: B) It removes soil and germs, leading to higher prices
D) It increases shelf life indefinitely
quiz.explanation: Clean produce looks professional and reduces spoilage, so buyers pay more.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration of salt for washing root crops?
quiz.explanation: A mild salt solution (1 tbsp per 10L) kills germs without harming produce.

quiz.q: How soon after harvest should you sort produce?
quiz.explanation: Sorting within 4 hours maintains freshness and reduces deterioration.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of grading produce?
options: B) It allows uniform pricing and higher value
C) It reduces the need for cleaning
quiz.explanation: Grading creates uniform categories that buyers prefer and pay more for.

quiz.q: Which tool can help grade avocados by size?
options: B) A measuring tape or template
quiz.explanation: Size grading uses diameter measurements, so a tape or template works.

quiz.q: What does Grade A produce typically mean?
quiz.explanation: Grade A is the highest quality, with no blemishes and uniform shape.

quiz.q: For maize, what simple test can check if it is dry enough?
quiz.explanation: If a kernel cracks when bitten, it indicates low moisture and readiness for storage.

quiz.q: Which container is best for transporting tomatoes to avoid crushing?
quiz.explanation: Plastic crates allow airflow and prevent crushing better than sacks.

quiz.q: What is a common capacity for a standard sack of grain?
quiz.explanation: A standard sack for grains like maize is typically 50 kg.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overfilling crates?
options: A) It makes them too heavy
B) It causes crushing and bruising
quiz.explanation: Overfilling leads to compression damage, reducing quality.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when stacking crates for transport?
options: A) Stack as high as possible
B) Stack no more than 4 high
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 4 high can crush the bottom crates and produce.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of post-harvest losses during transport?
quiz.explanation: Heat and rough handling cause bruising and spoilage during transport.

quiz.q: When is the best time to harvest to reduce transport losses?
options: B) Early morning or late evening
quiz.explanation: Cooler times of day reduce heat stress and spoilage.

quiz.q: What is evaporative cooling?
options: B) Wrapping produce in wet sacks
quiz.explanation: Evaporative cooling uses wet materials to lower temperature through evaporation.

quiz.q: Why should you not mix ripe fruits with vegetables during transport?
options: B) Ethylene from fruits speeds ripening of vegetables
quiz.explanation: Ethylene gas from ripe fruits can cause vegetables to ripen or spoil faster.

quiz.q: What is a simple way to label a sack of produce?
options: A) Write on the sack with permanent marker
B) Use a sticker or tag
quiz.explanation: Both writing directly and using tags are simple labeling methods.

quiz.q: What should a basic label include?
options: A) Farm name, produce type, grade, weight
quiz.explanation: Key details help buyers identify and trust your produce.

quiz.q: How can branding help a small farmer?
options: B) It builds recognition and can raise prices
quiz.explanation: A consistent brand builds customer loyalty and allows premium pricing.

quiz.q: What is a simple logo idea for a farm?
options: B) A drawing of a sun or leaf
quiz.explanation: Simple, recognizable symbols like a sun or leaf work well as logos.

quiz.q: Why is honest labeling important?
options: B) It builds trust and repeat business
C) It is required by law
quiz.explanation: Honest labels build a reputation for reliability, leading to repeat sales.

quiz.q: What should you do before planting to meet buyer quality requirements?
options: A) Ask the buyer what they want
quiz.explanation: Knowing buyer standards upfront allows you to plan production accordingly.

quiz.q: Which certification is often required for exporters?
quiz.explanation: GlobalG.A.P. is a common international standard for good agricultural practices.

quiz.q: What is traceability?
options: B) Ability to track produce from farm to buyer
quiz.explanation: Traceability means being able to trace the history of produce, important for quality and safety.

quiz.q: Why should you follow pre-harvest intervals for pesticides?
options: B) To ensure chemical residues are within safe limits
quiz.explanation: Pre-harvest intervals ensure pesticides break down before harvest, meeting safety standards.

quiz.q: What should you do if you cannot meet a buyer's quality standard?
options: B) Sell to a buyer with lower standards
quiz.explanation: Honesty and finding the right market prevents contract failures and reputational damage.

quiz.q: How can a farmer learn about buyer requirements?
options: A) Visit the buyer and ask questions
D) Wait for feedback after delivery
quiz.explanation: Direct communication with buyers clarifies expectations and standards.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of consistent quality?
options: A) Higher prices and repeat orders
quiz.explanation: Consistency builds trust, leading to better prices and loyal customers.

quiz.q: What simple tool can help grade eggs by weight?
quiz.explanation: Eggs are graded by weight, so a scale is essential.

quiz.q: Why is it important to clean and dry containers between uses?
options: A) To prevent disease and pests
B) To make them look new
quiz.explanation: Dirty containers can harbor pathogens and pests, contaminating new produce.

quiz.q: What is a key step to reduce post-harvest losses after transport?
options: A) Unpack immediately and store cool
quiz.explanation: Prompt unpacking and cool storage minimize further deterioration.
